nodes.label: Streamer
nodes.summary: Broadcasts from encoder software; the video arrives as RTMP at a nearby point of presence.

nodes.label: Viewer
nodes.summary: Watches the stream by fetching HLS playlists and segments over HTTP, and chats over an IRC-compatible connection.

nodes.label: PoP media proxy (Intelligest)
nodes.summary: Runs in every point of presence (nearly a hundred). Terminates the broadcaster's stream, asks IRS where to send it, and forwards it over the private backbone. Can terminate several transport protocols such as RTMP or WebRTC.

nodes.label: Intelligest Routing Service (IRS)
nodes.summary: Stateful controller in AWS that decides which origin processes each stream. Uses a randomized greedy algorithm over live capacity data and can pin channels to an origin. Does not control Layer 3 routing.

nodes.label: Capacitor
nodes.summary: Monitors the compute resources in every origin, including capacity that goes offline for maintenance.

nodes.label: The Well
nodes.summary: Monitors the backbone network: link utilization and availability.

nodes.label: Origin transcoding system
nodes.summary: Origin data centers host hundreds to thousands of servers that transcode the incoming RTMP stream into an HLS-compliant stream with several resolutions and bitrates. ASIC-based transcoding was prototyped for over 10x the scale.

nodes.label: Replication Tree (video distribution)
nodes.summary: Data centers organised as a directed graph hierarchy. A viewer's request goes to the nearest data center and is forwarded up the tree to the origin.
nodes.details: Caching behaviour and tree shape are not described in the posts we read.

nodes.label: VOD store (Amazon S3)
nodes.summary: If recording is enabled, a copy of all generated segments, thumbnails and playlists is stored in S3; streamers can cut highlights from it.

nodes.label: Chat system
nodes.summary: Real-time distributed system in Go that accepts, checks and fans out chat messages. Supports IRC so developers can build bots.

nodes.label: Chat Edge
nodes.summary: Accepts messages from clients and delivers messages to them. Speaks the IRC protocol over raw TCP and WebSockets.
nodes.details: Developer docs: the server sends PING and the client must answer PONG; chatbots are rate limited (20 messages per 30 seconds for a regular account, 1 per second per channel).

nodes.label: Clue (and Zuma)
nodes.summary: Evaluates a message against the channel's rules (automod settings, bans, subscriber status) and decides whether it is delivered or rejected.

nodes.label: Pubsub
nodes.summary: Distributes messages internally across Edge nodes; with Edge forms a hierarchical message distribution system that executes massive fanout.

nodes.label: Room
nodes.summary: Aggregates, stores and queries membership data across all edges to produce the viewer list of each chat room.

nodes.label: Alternative: low-latency HLS
nodes.summary: Partial segments, blocking playlist reload and preload hints let a player learn of new media at once instead of polling every target duration. Twitch says it cut delay from about 10 s to about 3 s with low-latency HLS; the exact mechanism in use is not described, so this is from the specification.

edges.label: fan out to edges with subscribers

flows.name: A stream goes live and is watched

steps.caption: The streamer's encoder sends RTMP video to the nearest point of presence.
The media proxy extracts the stream's properties and asks IRS which origin should process it.
IRS uses live compute capacity from Capacitor (and backbone status from The Well) to decide.
The proxy forwards the stream to the chosen origin over the private backbone.
The origin transcodes it into several qualities as HLS and sends it into the replication tree.
A viewer's player requests the playlist and segments from the nearest data center; a miss goes up the tree to the origin.
Capacitor reflects lost compute in an origin, for example servers offline.
A new stream arrives at a PoP and the proxy asks IRS where to send it.
IRS directs the new stream to an unaffected origin. The posts do not say how streams already on the failed origin recover.
The viewer's client sends a message to a chat edge.
The edge forwards it to Clue, which checks the channel's rules.
If accepted, the message is published to Pubsub.
Pubsub fans it out to every edge with subscribers for that channel.
Each edge delivers it to its connected clients.

flows.name: A message the rules reject (failure path)

steps.caption: Clue evaluates it against the channel's automod settings and the sender's status, and rejects it. It is never published, so no other viewer sees it.
